title: I Logged Every Disc-Golf Tee-Pad Minute the League Captain Called Overflow

parts.text: I stepped onto tee seven at 10:02 a.m. and captain Ellis was already putting from our numbered pad. The kiosk said: ONE TEE. TWELVE MINUTES. CARD STAYS WITH THE GROUP. I was thirty-one, club scorer, holding a card that listed our hole. Ellis shrugged. "Captains are overflow." I photographed the kiosk, the card, and his bag on our tee. Then I asked for the pad log. At 10:09 parks pinged why Ellis's name was on our twelve. I kept my voice park-quiet and let the timestamp talk. A kiosk is only a kiosk until someone treats it like a clock.
parts.cliffhanger_hint: Parks can see Ellis's bag on tee seven during our twelve minutes.

social.video_title: He putted from our numbered pad on our twelve — Part 1/2
social.description: Disc-golf tee, a captain on our pad, a twelve-minute clock he posted. I logged the putt. Would you have asked for the pad log?

parts.text: Ellis called it a practice until parks asked for the photo. I printed the ticket, the kiosk, and the bag still. The pad went back to our card. Ellis ran his own twelve and told the next captain atmosphere was always about flow. Flow is a word captains use when a card exists. Tee policy now has a second line: CAPTAINS ARE NOT OVERFLOW. I keep our card on a labeled clip. Ellis brown-bags his jokes. The tee finally looks like a group, not a loan. The rule looks ordinary now, which is the whole point.

social.description: Pad log, numbered tee, and a second line on the kiosk. Was practice ever our twelve?
